Great Lakes Cheese in Franklinville discharged toxic, nutrient-rich daily processing wastewater into Ischua Creek on Aug. 26, which killed thousands of fish and other wildlife. It wasn't the first time the company polluted the creek.
A fish kill in Ischua Creek has caused concern in Franklinville after officials confirmed that discharge from the Great Lakes Cheese facility is likely responsible for environmental damage.

Emails and other documents show what the state Department of Environmental Conservation knew about the pollution at Great Lakes Cheese in Franklinville before the massive fish die-off in August.

Tens of thousands of fish and other wildlife were killed last summer in Ischua Creek. New York state environmental regulators said they responded "immediately." But emails, other documents show the agency waited two weeks to take action and stop the toxic discharge coming from Great Lakes Cheese.
ICYMI: State officials knew the water in Ischua Creek could have been deadly for fish for at least two weeks before taking action to rein in pollution coming from Great Lakes Cheese in Franklinville.
The DEC says that it has directed the Great Lakes Cheese facility in Franklinville to take immediate actions to address ongoing impacts related to the discharge of organic waste to Ischua Creek.

For months, Great Lakes Cheese has been discharging polluted wastewater into Ischua Creek far in excess of what its permits allow, according to data from the Environmental Protection Agency.

The DEC announced Great Lakes Cheese has been ordered to pay $475,000 in penalties and take corrective actions related to discharge in Ischua Creek.
Great Lakes Cheese said it is containing and testing wastewater on site, and then it is being removed to permitted farms. No wastewater is being discharged into Ischua Creek at this time.

State regulators still aren't offering any details about what Great Lakes Cheese may have accidentally discharged into Ischua Creek, killing thousands of fish and badly polluting 8 miles of the waterway, a popular fishing spot.
